opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two things that often get lumped together under "the scaling hypothesis." One is the empirical observation, the scaling laws: if you increase compute, data, and parameters in the right proportions, the loss goes down in a very predictable, power-law way. That part, to me as a physicist, is remarkable, and it's held up over many orders of magnitude. When you see a clean straight line on a log-log plot across that many decades, you take it seriously. That's the kind of regularity that usually points to some underlying principle, even if we don't fully understand it yet.

The second thing is the stronger claim: that just continuing to push along that line gets you all the capabilities you care about. There I'd be a bit more careful. Lower loss on next-token prediction has correlated really well with things we care about, but the mapping from loss to capabilities isn't something we have a theory of. And the line itself has costs. Each step requires multiplicatively more compute, and at some point you run into very practical constraints like energy, chips, and the amount of high-quality data available.

What's been exciting recently is that people have found new axes to scale along. The clearest example is reasoning models, where you spend more compute at inference time, letting the model think longer, and you get another predictable improvement curve. So I'd say the scaling hypothesis in its general form, that more compute applied in the right way keeps buying you more intelligence, looks very healthy. The interesting research question is figuring out which "right ways" exist, and that's where I think a bit of theory, actually understanding why these systems scale the way they do, can help us find the next axis rather than just stumbling onto it.

So I'm bullish, but I think of scaling less as a single recipe and more as a principle: find the knob where more compute reliably turns into better results, and then turn it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I come at this as a physicist, and I think the honest answer is that scaling has been the single most reliable empirical fact we've had in this field. You take a transformer, you add more data, more compute, more parameters, and the loss goes down in a way that's smooth and predictable enough that you can actually write down an equation for it. For a physicist, that's remarkable. Most of machine learning historically did not look like that. It looked like a pile of tricks that sometimes worked.

So in that sense, I take the scaling hypothesis very seriously. The thing I'd push back on is the stronger version of it, which is that scaling alone is sufficient, that you just keep turning the crank and everything falls out. There are a couple of reasons I'm skeptical of that.

One is that the loss going down is not the same thing as the capability you care about going up. The scaling laws tell you about cross-entropy on the pretraining distribution. They don't tell you directly about whether the model can do multi-step reasoning or plan or avoid making things up. Sometimes those things improve with scale, sometimes they appear suddenly, and we don't really have a theory that predicts which is which.

The second is more practical. Pretraining compute scaling is hitting real constraints. Data is one, in the sense that the amount of high-quality text you can scrape is finite, and we're closer to the edge of that than people like to admit. And the compute itself is getting expensive enough that each order of magnitude is a serious capital decision rather than a research decision.

So what's happened in the last couple of years is that the scaling has shifted. It's moved from pretraining to things like reinforcement learning and test-time compute, where you let the model think longer or sample more. And interestingly, those seem to have their own scaling curves. That's actually what makes me optimistic. The lesson of scaling isn't "make the model bigger," it's "find a quantity you can increase smoothly that converts into capability." We found one with parameters and data. Now we're finding others.

So my assessment is something like: scaling is the engine, but it's not the map. It tells you that if you push, things improve. It doesn't tell you where the next push should go, and figuring that out is still genuinely a science problem. I'd like us to have a real theory of why these curves look the way they do, because right now we're mostly fitting power laws after the fact, and that's a little unsatisfying if you came up doing theoretical physics.

astra-6.text:
I think the scaling hypothesis is a very powerful working hypothesis, but we have to be precise about what we’re claiming. One claim is that if you increase compute, data, and model size in the right proportions, you get predictable improvements in the training objective. A stronger claim is that those improvements will translate into every capability we care about. That second step is much less certain.

The exciting thing is that a relatively simple objective can produce capabilities you didn’t explicitly build into the system. That gives us a good reason to keep exploring scale. But it doesn’t tell us how much compute a particular capability will require, or whether scaling the current approach is the most efficient way to get there.

So I’d keep pushing scale while also working on algorithms, data quality, and how we measure progress. Scaling gives us a direction. It doesn’t, by itself, give us a complete theory of intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scaling hypothesis has been remarkably successful, but we should be precise about what it says. We’ve seen that increasing compute, data, and model size in the right proportions leads to fairly predictable improvements in training loss. That’s a powerful empirical observation. It gives you a way to plan experiments and decide where to invest resources.

The harder question is how those improvements translate into the capabilities we care about. A lower loss doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether a system can reliably carry out a long task or discover something new. And extrapolating a trend assumes you can keep supplying the right data and compute without hitting a bottleneck.

So I’d take scaling very seriously as a path forward, but I wouldn’t treat it as a complete theory of intelligence. The interesting question is what we should scale—and what changes to learning, data, or inference make that scaling more effective.
